text: Dragnet is an American crime drama television series starring Jack Webb and Harry Morgan that aired for four seasons, from January 12, 1967, to April 16, 1970. To distinguish it from the earlier 1950s Dragnet series, the ending year of each season was included in the on-screen title, beginning as Dragnet 1967 and concluding as Dragnet 1970. The series aired every Thursday from 9:30 to 10:00 pm (ET) and was directed by Jack Webb. All four seasons have been released on DVD; Season 1 ("Dragnet 1967") was released by Universal Studios Home Entertainment, while Seasons 2 ("1968"), 3 ("1969"), and 4 ("1970") were released by Shout! Factory. This was the second television series in the Dragnet media franchise, which includes film, television, books, and comics, and it holds the distinction of being one of the first examples of a discontinued American TV series being revived years later with some original cast members. Actors who played multiple roles during the series include Don Ross, Olan Soule, Marco Lopez, Herb Vigran, Clark Howat, Art Balinger, Alfred Shelly, Art Gilmore, Ralph Moody, Virginia Gregg, Ed Deemer, Howard Culver, Bert Holland, Don Stewart, Bobby Troup, Len Wayland, William Boyett, Stacy Harris, Stuart Nisbet, Kent McCord, Robert Brubaker, Harry Bartell, Jill Banner, Robert Patten, Sidney Clute, Anthony Eisley, Virginia Vincent, Don Dubbins, James McEachin, Peggy Webber, Jack Sheldon, and Vic Perrin. Each episode typically begins with stock footage of Los Angeles followed by Sgt. Joe Friday’s introduction, "This is the city," after which he specifies the day and time and describes the watch or shift he and Gannon are working. Friday, usually the lead investigator, and Gannon investigate each case, with Friday maintaining a polite but terse, clipped, and rigid manner of questioning witnesses or suspects, often responding to irrelevant details with, "Ma’am (Sir), we just want to get the facts." At the end of each episode, the legal fate of the arrested suspects is revealed. Friday and Gannon are rarely shown outside their professional relationship; Gannon occasionally mentions his wife, Eileen, and family, and sometimes encourages Friday, who is single, to have a social life. In a rare departure from the crime drama, the 1968 episode "Homicide: DR-06" shows Friday inviting the Gannons to his apartment for a steak dinner, only to have the evening repeatedly interrupted by other tenants seeking his assistance. In 1965, Jack Webb was approached by Universal Pictures to produce a Dragnet television movie for NBC; NBC programming director Mort Werner was impressed and decided to develop Dragnet into a weekly series. Webb was initially more interested in continuing the franchise with TV movies but ultimately agreed. The movie, which had a working title of Dragnet 1966, was released on January 27, 1969 (midway through the third season) on The NBC Monday Movie under the promotional title World Premiere: Dragnet, and is commonly referred to as Dragnet 1966 to distinguish it from other franchise works. It is included as an extra in the Dragnet 1968 DVD set. All episodes of the series were directed by Jack Webb. In one episode, Friday and Gannon investigate a bank robbery committed by a man and a woman; tracking their car leads them to a woman who matches the suspect’s description, initially lies to them, and is already on probation, leading the detectives to believe they have a suspect—until additional reports reveal other women being forced to rob banks in the same way. Though the first woman is cleared, the spree continues until one victim fights back. Sergeant Carl Maxwell, a fellow detective, goes AWOL after a case he worked on is dismissed; Friday and Gannon are given three days to find him before he is terminated from the LAPD. When they locate him drinking at a resort, he rants about the stresses of policing and claims he is a minority for being a cop, but a speech from Friday convinces him to return. Friday and Gannon also investigate an officer accused of police brutality following a drunk driving arrest; officers Pete Malloy (Martin Milner) and Jim Reed (Kent McCord), the main characters of Adam-12, appear as witnesses. In another episode, 17-year-old Hal Rustin (Michael Burns) is a car thief whose mother, Eunice Rustin (Peggy Webber), is unable to stop him. He is given a tour of jail to illustrate the consequences of crime, but it fails, and he later kills someone with a shotgun. Note: Harry Morgan had a bloody nose the night before filming.
